sn11.8:1.1: This discourse poses a number of interpretive difficulties, apparently because it responds to the culminating dialogue of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.7–12). There, Virocana studies with Indra under their Progenitor, Prajāpati, to learn about the higher Self that is free from evil and death.
sn11.8:1.3: Verocana is “son of Virocana (Agni or the Sun). He is called Bali at [dn20:12.9](). His story is detailed in various legends of later times. He was a great king of the titans who at times even defeated the gods and ruled heaven, but did so justly. Here he seems to have settled his long enmity with Indra.
sn11.8:2.1: The Upaniṣad says the “highest man” (_uttamapuruṣa_) is the one who rises up from his body and manifests in his own form as the perfect light (8.12.3).
sn11.8:2.2: The Sutta substitutes _attha_ (“goal, purpose, good”) for the Upaniṣad’s _ātman_ (“Self”) in line with the dictum, “the goal is spoken of, but the self is not involved” ([an3.72:6.3](), [an6.49:4.3]()). | For _nipphadā_ (“accomplishment”), Pali normally uses the prefixed form _abhinipphanna_ (“produced, manifested”) in this sense ([mn101:29.3](), [sn47.10:6.11]()). And that is the form the root appears in the Upaniṣad, in the sense of the Self that “achieves” or “emerges into” in its own true form (8.12.2).
sn11.8:2.3: Pali texts read this phrase as either _nipphannasobhano attho_ (nominative singular) or _nipphannasobhino atthā_ (dative singular). I propose both phrases are found, as suits each speaker. The titan Verocana makes a banal assertion and brands it as his own wisdom. The god Sakka improves it by pointing to the cause, echoing [sn11.4:7.3](). This echoes the narrative form of Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7–12, where Virocana is easily satisfied with surface teachings, taking only the body to be the Self. | The “splendid” or “shining” (_sobhana_) goal recalls the “highest light” (_paraṃ jyotir_) of the manifest Self.
sn11.8:2.4: Verocana asserts his authorship of this rather banal observation. He is imitating the Upaniṣad, which repeatedly states, “this is the word of Prajāpati” (_iti ha prajāpatir uvāca_, 8.12.6).
sn11.8:3.4: Indra and Virocana spent 32 years as Prajāpati’s students. Satisfied, Virocana left, while Indra stayed for a total of 101 years. Only then did Prajāpati reward his patience by revealing the deep truth.
sn11.8:4.1: In the Upaniṣad, “all” qualifies that which is to be attained, namely all worlds and all desires (8.12.6). | Text has _sattā_ (“beings”) and _pāṇi_ (“creature”) for the Upaniṣad’s _bhūta_ (8.11.1; also _sarvabhūtāni_ at 8.15.1).
sn11.8:4.2: In other words, all creatures have individual and differing needs (see [an4.32:2.4](), [dn31:34.24]()).
sn11.8:4.3: For _saṁyoga_, compare the Upaniṣad, “The lifebreath is yoked to this body, as a draft animal to a cart” (_sa yathā prayogya ācaraṇe yukta evam evāyam asmiñ charīre prāṇo yuktaḥ_, 8.12.3, translation Olivelle). This shows the original meaning of root _yuj_ as “yoke” for beasts of burden, and hence the “work” those beasts do. Other meanings such as “combination” or “association” introduce new ideas, whereas this sense sticks to Verocana’s message of doing the work.
sn11.8:4.4: When, in the Upaniṣad, Indra rejects lower teachings of the Self, he says he sees in it nothing “worthwhile” (_bhogya_), corresponding to _sambhoga_ here.
